narrative:
The model estimates you have a 49% chance of leaving your job, which is high enough that the company has decided to deny your promotion. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors in your profile.

Your relatively short overall work experience of 1-5 years was the strongest influence pulling the prediction toward leaving. Among employees the model expected to stay, only about half had similarly limited experience, while the rest had six or more years. This lack of broader career history made the system less confident in your long-term commitment.

The fact that you have received other job offers while working here was the second most important factor and pushed the prediction in the opposite direction, toward staying. Having external opportunities often signals that an employee is valued in the market, which the model sees as a reason you might remain.

Your employment in the medical sector was the third strongest influence and worked in favor of staying. Medical roles form a large portion of employees the model predicted would stay, suggesting the sector itself is associated with greater stability.

Taken together, your limited experience outweighed the stabilizing effects of external offers and your sector, tipping the balance toward likely departure. The organization should consider giving promising early-career staff clearer development paths and faster recognition. You may want to discuss your career goals openly with your manager to strengthen your connection to the role. (248 words)
